answers.question: List of scenarios
answers.evidence: "Oceania Scenario name: Orderly / Disorderly / Hothouse World … Alignment to Sector Scenarios: Health Sector – Ambitious and Orderly / Delayed and Disorderly / Hothouse World; Property and Construction Sector – Orderly / Disorderly / Hothouse World … Scenario archetypes used by Sector Scenarios: Network for Greening the Financial System … Net Zero 2050 (1.5°C) / Delayed Transition / Current Policies"
answers.notes: Three scenarios used: Orderly, Disorderly, and Hothouse World, aligned to NGFS archetypes and sector-specific scenario names.

answers.question: Global temperature outcome by 2100
answers.answer: Three temperature outcomes by 2100: <1.5°C (Orderly), ~2.7°C (Disorderly), >3°C (Hothouse World). No temperature overshoot is described.
answers.evidence: "Global temperature outcomes: <1.5°C / ~2.7°C / >3°C … Note RCP2.6 formed the lower bound of the physical risk assessment and hence is associated with an Orderly scenario insofar as RCP2.6 is associated with a ~1.5°C warming above pre-industrial levels, by 2100 … The Disorderly scenario describes a hypothetical world where warming is approximately 2.7°C by 2100."
answers.notes: Temperature outcomes are explicitly stated in the scenario description table and footnotes.

answers.question: Scenario provider
answers.answer: Multiple scenario providers are explicitly named: (1) Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) – for scenario archetypes; (2) IPCC (AR6 for global narrative; AR5 for NIWA's downscaled physical risk data); (3) NIWA – for downscaled physical risk data; (4) New Zealand Green Business Council (NZGBC) / Beca – for the Construction and Property Sector Scenarios; (5) Sustainable Healthcare Aotearoa / Tonkin + Taylor – for the Health Sector Scenarios; (6) Climate Change Commission (CCC) – Tailwinds, Headwinds and Current Policies scenarios; (7) IEA – World Outlook Energy scenarios.
answers.evidence: "These Sector Scenarios aligned with the International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and the Climate Change Commission's Tailwinds, Headwinds and Current Policies scenarios. The Construction and Property Sector Scenarios also aligned with the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) archetypes of Orderly, Disorderly and Hothouse World, as well as the IEA World Outlook Energy scenarios." and "IPCC scenario (AR6) for global narrative / IPCC scenario (AR5) for NIWA's downscaled physical risk data"
answers.notes: Multiple providers named. The sector scenarios were facilitated by Beca (Construction & Property) and Tonkin + Taylor (Health Sector).
answers.ani_notes: The Construction and Property Sector Scenarios; NGFS; IPCC SSP-RCP;

answers.question: Pick-and-mix of SSPs and RCPs
answers.evidence: "IPCC scenario (AR6) for global narrative: Net Zero 2050 (1.5°C) – IPCC SSP1-1.9 / RCP2.6; Delayed Transition – IPCC SSP2-4.5 / RCP4.5; Current Policies – IPCC SSP3-7.0 / RCP8.5 … Note RCP2.6 formed the lower bound of the physical risk assessment … NIWA has not downscaled SSP1-1.9 for New Zealand and the closest downscaled scenario is SSP1-2.6."
answers.notes: The document explicitly lists both SSP identifiers (from IPCC AR6) and RCP identifiers (from IPCC AR5, used for NIWA's downscaled physical risk data). SSPs and RCPs are from different IPCC assessment report generations (AR6 and AR5 respectively), constituting a pick-and-mix approach. The document itself acknowledges this: "NIWA has not downscaled SSP1-1.9 for New Zealand and the closest downscaled scenario is SSP1-2.6."

answers.question: Customised scenarios
answers.evidence: "Oceania's scenario narratives incorporate various elements of the Sector Scenarios. For example, narrative from the Property and Construction Sector Scenario relating to energy and electricity demand and changes to building regulations and supply chain, and narrative from the Health Sector scenarios relating to communities, the effects of global trade volatility, rising costs for senior citizens and technological advancements in care. Where applicable, these narrative elements have been adapted or expanded to reflect the specific context of the aged care sector."
answers.notes: Scenarios were adapted from sector-level scenarios (Construction & Property and Health Sector) and further tailored to the aged care context. NIWA downscaled physical risk data was also used for New Zealand-specific projections.
answers.ani_notes: Yes, Oceania's climate scenarios then incorporate driving forces and critical uncertainties prioritised specifically to Oceania, allowing it to test the resilience of its business model and strategy to climaterelated risks and opportunities.

answers.question: Co-produced climate scenarios
answers.answer: Yes – Oceania participated as a member of Technical Working Groups for both the Construction and Property Sector Scenarios and the Health Sector Scenarios, contributing to their co-development.
answers.evidence: "Oceania contributed to the development of climate-related scenarios for both the Construction and Property Sector, and the Health Sector (together, the Sector Scenarios), participating as a member of the respective Technical Working Groups."
answers.notes: Oceania's entity-level scenario analysis also involved internal workshops with management and subject matter experts: "Oceania's entity level scenario analysis process was conducted with input from management and subject matter experts including clinical, operational and functional expertise. Across a series of workshops, with executive sponsorship from the CFO..."
answers.ani_notes: Yes. Oceania participated as a member of the Technical Working Group in the development  of climate scenarios on behalf of the construction and property sector coordinated by the New Zealand Green Business Council (NZGBC) and facilitated by Beca, in 2022- 2023. participated as a member of the Technical Working Group in the development of climate scenarios on behalf of the healthcare sector, which were facilitated by Tonkin+Taylor (Climate Scenarios for the Healthcare Sector).

answers.question: Baseline scenarios
answers.answer: No explicit standalone baseline/reference scenario is described. However, the "Current Policies" scenario (aligned to IPCC SSP3-7.0 / RCP8.5 / Hothouse World) functions as a high-warming reference point, and the Climate Change Commission's "Current Policies" scenario is referenced as one of the scenario alignments.
answers.evidence: "These Sector Scenarios aligned with the International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and the Climate Change Commission's Tailwinds, Headwinds and Current Policies scenarios." and "Current Policies – IPCC SSP3-7.0 / RCP8.5"
answers.notes: The document does not describe a formal baseline scenario against which the climate scenarios are explicitly compared. The "Current Policies" label is used as one of three scenario archetypes, not as a dedicated baseline. The physical risk assessment uses RCP8.5 as the basis for long-term exposure assessment.

This dataset is based on the global IPCC AR6 projections and includes modelled inundation polygons" … "MfE, Auckland Climate Projections Map, using SSP1-2.6" … "These outcomes were calculated using Green Star and Homestar energy models." … "Oceania has not performed additional modelling beyond that used to create the international archetypes, which Oceania relied on to develop the Sector Scenarios."

answers.question: Damage from acute physical risk considered
answers.evidence: "Risk of acute weather events on infrastructure and property: As acute extreme weather events become increasingly frequent and intense, this may cause significant or sustained damage to Oceania land and buildings, as well as critical infrastructure such as power, water and telecommunications that support Oceania's villages … Oceania's assets at risk include site roading, cladding and components, basements, carparks, storage of critical infrastructure, lifts, roofing, guttering, fences, gas and water pipes, shifting foundations, paint and flashings. The range of reasonably anticipated impacts to operations include: outages to power, water and communications; disruption to site access; evacuation and need for temporary accommodation; loss of revenue; impact on resident and employee experience and wellbeing; increased remedial and operational costs (direct and indirect costs, such as insurance)."
answers.notes: The scenario analysis explicitly includes damage/loss estimates from acute extreme weather events (sea surge, storms, flooding, drought, landslides, high winds, wildfires). The physical risk assessment also quantifies the percentage of portfolio exposed to coastal inundation, river/surface flooding, coastal erosion, and landslides.
answers.ani_notes: Yes; Increasing frequency and intensity of extreme weather events including cyclones, storms and flooding

answers.question: Time frames
answers.answer: Short-term: present day to 2030; Medium-term: 2031–2050; Long-term: 2051–2080. Rationales are explicitly provided for each timeframe.
answers.evidence: "Short-term: Present day – 2030 – Aligns with Oceania's near-term capital allocation and funding cycle, Oceania's refurbishment cycles and process, near-term GHG reduction targets, and the need for global emissions to halve by 2030. Medium-term: 2031 – 2050 – Aligns with capital allocation for next wave of Oceania's funding strategy, home ownership trends, evolution of human capital elements, NZ and global net zero by 2050 ambitions. Long-term: 2051 – 2080 – Aligns with ownership and operation of long-lived assets subject to the long-term impacts of climate change, building conversion trends, and design lifespans."
answers.notes: Rationales are explicitly provided for all three timeframes. The document also notes the long-term horizon (2051–2080) is shorter than the Sector Scenarios which extended to 2100.

answers.question: Justification for scenario/model choice
answers.evidence: "These three scenarios were chosen because they cover a plausible range of futures and, therefore, are useful to test and identify a range of physical and transition risks and opportunities under different levels of uncertainty. While Oceania's scenario analysis includes a 1.5°C (Orderly scenario) pathway in compliance with NZ CS 1, it acknowledges that current global emissions trajectories and recent temperature records suggest that limiting warming to 1.5°C is becoming increasingly challenging."
answers.notes: Justification is provided for the choice of three scenarios (plausible range of futures, regulatory compliance with NZ CS 1). The document also explains why specific SSP/RCP combinations were used (e.g. NIWA has not downscaled SSP1-1.9 so SSP1-2.6/RCP2.6 was used instead).
answers.ani_notes: Yes. Oceania chose these three scenarios as they provided the opportunity to test a range of possible risks and opportunities under different levels of uncertainty.

answers.question: Historic climate impacts
answers.answer: Yes – the document references the 2023 Auckland Anniversary weekend floods and Cyclone Gabrielle as historical weather events that contributed to pressure on the New Zealand insurance market, with ongoing (immaterial) effects on Oceania's insurance cover, premiums and policy excesses.
answers.evidence: "The weather events of 2023, such as the Auckland Anniversary weekend floods and Cyclone Gabrielle, contributed to pressure on the New Zealand insurance market. In FY25, Oceania continued to experience the effects, albeit immaterial, of weather-related events on its insurance cover, premiums and, to a related extent, policy excesses."
answers.location_hint: Page 10 (Current climate-related impacts – Transition impacts: Insurance)
answers.notes: The document also states "Oceania did not experience material physical climate-related impacts in FY25." The historical impacts are described as transition impacts (insurance market pressure) rather than direct physical damage to Oceania's own assets.

answers.question: Direct and indirect physical climate risks
answers.evidence: Direct: "Risk of acute weather events on infrastructure and property: As acute extreme weather events become increasingly frequent and intense, this may cause significant or sustained damage to Oceania land and buildings … Oceania's assets at risk include site roading, cladding and components, basements, carparks, storage of critical infrastructure, lifts, roofing, guttering, fences, gas and water pipes, shifting foundations, paint and flashings." Indirect: "Risk of acute and/or chronic climate hazards on supply chain: A range of climate hazards (both acute and chronic) cause significant and ongoing disruption to Oceania's supply chain … disruption to essential supplies (and associated labour); delays to construction; disruption to community infrastructure (including roading access to Oceania's sites)."
answers.notes: The document explicitly considers both direct physical risks (damage to Oceania's own buildings, infrastructure, and property) and indirect physical risks (supply chain disruption, community infrastructure, insurance market effects from weather events affecting the broader market).
answers.ani_notes: Both; Potential delays from, and disruption to, supply chain and development (build/construction)activity.
